content: In many cells, the centrosome is situated in the cytoplasm, outside the nucleus. Microtubules cannot attach to chromatids when the nuclear envelope is intact. Therefore, during the early stages of the cell cycle, starting in prophase and continuing until approximately prometaphase, the nuclear membrane is dismantled. Concurrently, the nuclear lamina is also disassembled, a process regulated by the phosphorylation of lamin proteins. Toward the end of the cell cycle, the nuclear membrane is reformed, and the nuclear lamina is reassembled through the dephosphorylation of lamins. Apoptosis is a regulated process in which the structural components of a cell are systematically destroyed, leading to cell death. During apoptosis, changes occur that directly affect the nucleus and its contents, such as chromatin condensation and the disintegration of the nuclear envelope and lamina. The destruction of the lamin network is controlled by specialized apoptotic proteases called caspases, which cleave lamin proteins, thereby compromising the structural integrity of the nucleus. Lamin cleavage is sometimes used as a laboratory marker to indicate caspase activity in assays for early apoptotic events. Cells expressing mutant lamin proteins resistant to caspase cleavage exhibit deficiencies in nuclear changes associated with apoptosis, suggesting that lamins play a role in initiating the events leading to the apoptotic degradation of the nucleus. Furthermore, inhibition of lamin assembly itself can induce apoptosis. The nuclear envelope serves as a barrier that prevents both DNA and RNA viruses from entering the nucleus. However, some viruses require access to nuclear proteins for replication and/or assembly. DNA viruses, such as herpesviruses, replicate and assemble within the cell nucleus and exit by budding through the inner nuclear membrane. This process involves the disassembly of the lamina on the nuclear-facing side of the inner membrane. Although most cells contain a single nucleus, some cell types are anucleated, while others are multinucleated. Anucleated cells, such as mature mammalian red blood cells (erythrocytes), lack a nucleus and are incapable of dividing to produce daughter cells. Erythrocytes also lack other organelles, such as mitochondria, and primarily function as transport vessels for oxygen delivery from the lungs to tissues. Erythrocytes mature through erythropoiesis in the bone marrow, during which they lose their nuclei, organelles, and ribosomes. The nucleus is expelled during the differentiation process from an erythroblast to a reticulocyte, the immediate precursor to the mature erythrocyte. Exposure to mutagens may result in the release of immature, micronucleated erythrocytes into the bloodstream. Anucleated cells can also arise from defective cell division, where one daughter cell lacks a nucleus, and the other becomes binucleated. Multinucleated cells contain multiple nuclei. Certain protozoa, such as Acantharea, and some fungi in mycorrhizae naturally exhibit multinucleation. In humans, skeletal muscle cells (myocytes) become multinucleated during development. The peripheral arrangement of nuclei in these cells maximizes intracellular space for myofibrils. Abnormal multinucleated cells can also form in humans, such as giant multinucleated cells arising from the fusion of monocytes and macrophages. These cells are sometimes associated with inflammation and have been implicated in tumor formation. The evolutionary origin of the nucleus, a defining feature of eukaryotic cells, has been the subject of extensive speculation. Four major theories have been proposed, though none have gained widespread acceptance. The syntrophic model suggests that a symbiotic relationship between archaea and bacteria led to the formation of the nucleus-containing eukaryotic cell. This theory posits that ancient archaea, similar to modern methanogenic archaea, invaded and coexisted with bacteria resembling modern myxobacteria, eventually forming the early nucleus. This model is analogous to the widely accepted theory for the origin of mitochondria and chloroplasts, which are thought to have arisen from endosymbiotic relationships between proto-eukaryotes and aerobic bacteria. The archaeal origin of the nucleus is supported by similarities in certain genes, such as those encoding histones, between archaea and eukaryotes. Observations of myxobacteria, which are motile, form multicellular complexes, and possess kinases and G proteins similar to those in eukaryotes, support a bacterial origin for the eukaryotic cell. A second model proposes that proto-eukaryotic cells evolved from bacteria without an endosymbiotic stage. This model is based on the existence of modern planctomycetes bacteria, which possess a nuclear structure with primitive pores and other compartmentalized membrane structures. A related hypothesis suggests that a eukaryote-like cell, termed the chronocyte, evolved first and subsequently phagocytosed archaea and bacteria, leading to the development of the nucleus and the eukaryotic cell. The most controversial model, known as viral eukaryogenesis, posits that the membrane-bound nucleus and other eukaryotic features originated from the infection of a prokaryote by a virus. This hypothesis is based on similarities between eukaryotes and viruses, such as linear DNA strands, mRNA capping, and tight binding to proteins (analogous to histones and viral envelopes). One version of this proposal suggests that the nucleus evolved in conjunction with phagocytosis to form an early cellular predator. Another variant proposes that eukaryotes originated from early archaea infected by poxviruses, based on observed similarities between the DNA polymerases of modern poxviruses and eukaryotes. It has also been suggested that the unresolved question of the evolution of sexual reproduction could be related to the viral eukaryogenesis hypothesis. Finally, a recent proposal, termed the exomembrane hypothesis, argues that traditional variants of the endosymbiont theory are insufficient to explain the origin of the eukaryotic nucleus. This model suggests that the nucleus originated from a single ancestral cell that evolved a second exterior cell membrane. The interior membrane, enclosing the original cell, subsequently became the nuclear membrane and developed increasingly elaborate pore structures to facilitate the passage of internally synthesized cellular components, such as ribosomal subunits.
